name: Guyanese Pepperpot (Cassareep Meat Stew)
region: Guyana / Indigenous Amazonian and Caribbean foodways
time: 3 hrs 45 min, plus optional overnight rest
imageAlt: Dark Guyanese pepperpot with slow-braised meat and glossy cassareep gravy served in a bowl
imageCredit: Photo: Simon Abrams, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
summary: Guyanese pepperpot slowly braises beef and oxtail in cassareep with cinnamon, cloves, thyme and hot pepper until the meat is tender and the gravy turns dark, glossy and bittersweet.
lead: Commercially prepared cassareep gives this Guyanese Christmas classic its defining dark color, bittersweet depth and aroma, while a long, gentle simmer softens collagen-rich cuts of meat.
about: Pepperpot is one of Guyana's most recognized dishes and is especially associated with Christmas morning, when it is commonly eaten with plait bread. Its essential ingredient is cassareep, a dark, concentrated sauce made from cassava juice and long used in Indigenous foodways across Guyana and the wider Amazon region. Cinnamon, cloves, hot pepper and slow-cooked meat round out the pot. Families choose different combinations of beef, oxtail, cow heel, pork and other cuts; this home version uses beef chuck and oxtail for accessible texture and body.
story: Guyanese writer Indranie Deolall traces cassareep to Indigenous practice and records the Lokono word kashiripo for the concentrated cassava preparation. Historical pepperpots were replenished and reheated repeatedly, and cassareep was valued both for flavor and perceived keeping qualities. Contemporary food-safety guidance, however, makes refrigeration the sound home practice. Pepperpot remains living holiday food rather than a museum formula: the meat blend, sweetness, aromatics and heat shift from household to household, but cassareep, whole warm spices and patient braising identify the Guyanese dish.
caveat: Use only bottled cassareep produced for cooking. Never try to make it by simply squeezing or reducing raw bitter cassava at home; improperly processed cassava can contain dangerous cyanogenic compounds. Molasses or browning sauce can darken a stew but cannot replace cassareep's flavor. Although some traditional accounts describe keeping pepperpot at room temperature and reboiling it daily, this recipe follows modern safety practice: cool promptly, refrigerate within 2 hours and reheat only the portion you will serve.
prepNotes: Brands vary in salt, sugar and intensity. Begin with 1/2 cup in the pot, then add the remaining 1/4 cup only after the liquid has simmered and can be tasted safely.
A whole unbroken Scotch bonnet or wiri wiri perfumes the stew with controlled heat. Piercing or splitting it makes the pot dramatically hotter.
Oxtail needs time, not a hard boil. Hold the pot at a lazy simmer until connective tissue softens and the meat pulls easily from the bone.
ingredients: 2 lb boneless beef chuck, cut into 2-inch pieces
1 1/2 lb oxtail pieces, trimmed of large exterior fat
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
1/2 to 3/4 cup commercially prepared Guyanese cassareep
3 tbsp packed dark brown sugar, plus more only if needed
1 strip orange peel, about 3 inches long, with little white pith
1 whole Scotch bonnet or 3 whole wiri wiri peppers, left unbroken
5 to 6 cups hot water, or enough to barely cover the meat
Guyanese plait bread or another sturdy white bread, for serving
steps: Pat the beef and oxtail very dry. Season with 1 teaspoon salt and the black pepper, then let the meat stand while the onion and garlic are prepared.

Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a heavy 6- to 8-quart Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in two batches, turning until several sides are deeply colored, 6 to 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a bowl and repeat with the oxtail, adding the remaining oil if the pot looks dry.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion and cook 5 minutes, scraping up the browned film, until translucent and lightly golden. Stir in the garlic for 45 seconds, just until fragrant.

Return all meat and accumulated juices to the pot. Add 1/2 cup cassareep, brown sugar, cinnamon, cloves, thyme, orange peel and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Turn the meat until every piece is coated dark brown.
Pour in enough hot water to barely cover the meat. Bring to a full boil for 2 minutes, then reduce immediately to a very gentle simmer. Skim the first foam and excess surface fat.

Set the whole unbroken hot pepper on top. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and simmer 2 hours, turning the meat every 30 minutes. Add hot water in small amounts only if pieces rise well above the liquid.

After 2 hours, check the oxtail. Continue simmering 45 to 75 minutes, until a fork twists easily in the beef and the oxtail meat begins to pull from the bones. Remove the whole pepper before it splits; discard it or serve separately for diners who want more heat.

Taste a spoonful of cooled gravy. Add the remaining cassareep a tablespoon at a time for more characteristic bitterness and depth, or a small pinch of brown sugar if the brand is unusually sharp. The finished gravy should be dark and glossy, lightly thickened by gelatin, and balanced between savory, bittersweet, warm-spiced and hot.

Remove the cinnamon sticks, cloves where visible, thyme stems and orange peel. If serving the same day, rest the covered pot 20 minutes, skim excess fat and bring it back to a simmer before ladling with bread.

For deeper flavor, cool the stew in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours. The next day, remove the firm fat, return the stew to a clean pot and bring it to a rolling boil before lowering to a simmer for 10 minutes; the meat must reach 165°F throughout.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly for up to 4 days or freeze in meal-size containers. Do not rely on cassareep or daily boiling as a substitute for refrigeration.

difficultyReason: Requires browning in batches, controlling a long gentle braise, balancing a variable cassareep product and cooling or reheating the large pot safely.

name: Somali Baasto iyo Suugo (Pasta with Beef Sauce)
region: Somalia and Somali diaspora / Horn of Africa
type: Pasta with Spiced Meat Sauce / Main
category: Spaghetti with xawaash-spiced beef and tomato sauce
imageAlt: Somali baasto iyo suugo with spaghetti, rich xawaash-spiced beef tomato sauce and a banana served alongside
imageCredit: Photo: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
summary: Somali baasto iyo suugo pairs spaghetti with a tomato-rich beef sauce seasoned with aromatic xawaash, then serves lime and ripe banana alongside for savory, sour and sweet contrast.
lead: The familiar shape of spaghetti carries a distinctly Somali sauce: beef, tomato and green pepper simmer with xawaash, while lime and banana complete the plate rather than functioning as novelty garnishes.
about: Baasto iyo suugo means pasta and sauce in Somali. Baasto is a Somali borrowing from Italian pasta, while iyo means and; suugo names the tomato-based sauce. Somali cook and author Hawa Hassan describes suugo as the country's most popular pasta sauce, distinguished by xawaash, a warm spice blend. The sauce can use ground beef, turkey or chicken and can be served over several pasta shapes. Spaghetti with a ripe banana on the side is a widely recognized Somali way of eating the dish.
story: Italian colonial rule in southern Somalia left pasta in the food landscape, but Somali cooks made it their own rather than preserving an Italian dish unchanged. Xawaash, onion, garlic, green pepper and tomato shift the sauce's center of gravity toward the Somali pantry. The USDA now documents baasto iyo suugo as a staple in many Somali-American households, showing how the dish continues to travel and adapt in diaspora kitchens. Recipes differ on meat texture, spice ratios and whether pasta is tossed with the sauce or served beneath it; the banana-and-lime accompaniment supplies the sweet and sour contrast many households expect.
caveat: Xawaash is a family of Somali spice blends, not one universally fixed formula. This recipe gives a restrained home blend modeled on published versions; a trusted Somali-made blend can replace it measure for measure. Ground beef produces suugo, a cohesive meat sauce. Cubed meat sautéed more dryly is often called suqaar and should not be presented as exactly the same preparation. The banana is served alongside so diners can alternate bites rather than mash it automatically into the pasta.
prepNotes: Bloom, do not burn, the xawaash
Ground spices become fragrant in about 30 seconds. Have the tomato paste ready because scorched cardamom and cinnamon make the entire sauce bitter.
The tomato liquid should reduce until it clings to the beef and coats a spoon without a watery ring.
A small splash emulsifies the sauce around the spaghetti; plain water thins it without the same body.
ingredients: 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil or canola oil
1 small green bell pepper, finely chopped
1 lb ground beef, preferably 85 percent lean
1 1/4 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus salt for pasta water
1 can diced tomatoes with juices, 28 oz
3 ripe bananas, peeled and halved crosswise at serving time
steps: Mix the cumin, coriander, cardamom, turmeric, cinnamon, cloves and black pepper in a small bowl. This makes about 3 tablespoons xawaash; keep it beside the stove.

Heat the oil in a wide heavy skillet or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the red onion and green pepper and cook 7 to 9 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and beginning to brown at the edges.

Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds. Stir in the xawaash for another 30 seconds, just until the spices smell warm and floral. Immediately add the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes, stirring until it darkens to brick red.

Add the ground beef and 1 teaspoon salt. Break it into small pieces and cook 8 to 10 minutes, until no pink remains and browned bits form rather than a pool of gray liquid. If the pan becomes crowded and wet, raise the heat briefly and let moisture evaporate.
Add the diced tomatoes with their juices and 1 cup water. Scrape the bottom thoroughly, bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle uncovered simmer.

Simmer 25 to 30 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until the tomatoes have collapsed and the sauce is thick enough to mound briefly on a spoon. Checkpoint: oil may glisten at the edges, but there should be no raw tomato smell or watery layer.

While the sauce simmers, bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Add the spaghetti and cook until al dente according to the package, stirring during the first minute. Reserve 1 cup pasta water, then drain.

Taste the sauce and add the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt if needed. Stir in half the cilantro. If the sauce feels stiff, add reserved pasta water 2 tablespoons at a time until it coats the noodles without running to the bottom of the plate.
Add the spaghetti to the sauce and toss over low heat for 1 to 2 minutes, or plate the noodles and spoon suugo generously over each serving. Either service is used in home cooking.
Finish with the remaining cilantro. Serve each plate with lime wedges and half a ripe banana on the side; alternate bites of pasta and banana and squeeze lime over the sauce to taste.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours for up to 4 days. Reheat the sauce with a splash of water until bubbling and 165°F, and cook fresh pasta when possible for the best texture.

difficultyReason: Uses straightforward stovetop pasta and meat-sauce techniques, with the main judgment points being blooming the xawaash and reducing the tomatoes without scorching.

name: Cambodian Num Banh Chok (Khmer Rice Noodles)
type: Rice Noodles with Fish Gravy / Breakfast or Lunch
category: Rice noodles with kroeung-scented fish gravy and raw vegetables
imageAlt: Cambodian num banh chok rice noodles with pale fish gravy, fresh herbs, sliced vegetables and edible flowers
imageCredit: Photo: Thomas Wanhoff, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
summary: Cambodian num banh chok serves soft rice noodles with a light fish gravy pounded with lemongrass, turmeric, galangal and prahok, plus a generous tangle of crisp vegetables and herbs.
lead: Fresh noodles, a fragrant yellow-green fish gravy and a full platter of raw vegetables meet in one of Cambodia's defining breakfast dishes.
about: Num banh chok names both Cambodia's lightly fermented rice noodles and the dishes built around them. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation included Num Banh Chok Khmer in The Taste of Angkor, using freshwater fish, kroeung, coconut milk, prahok, palm sugar, fish sauce and an assortment of raw vegetables. Fresh Cambodian noodles are ideal, but refrigerated Vietnamese bun or dried medium rice vermicelli make a transparent home-kitchen substitution when specialist-made num banh chok is unavailable.
story: Across Cambodia, noodle makers traditionally soak, grind and ferment rice before pressing the dough into boiling water, while vendors sell the finished noodles with regional gravies and vegetables. Num banh chok is often shorthand for Khmer noodles, yet it is not a single fixed bowl: samlor Khmer, samlor proher, red curry and regional versions vary in herbs, fish, coconut and accompaniments. This recipe follows the pale fish-and-kroeung route promoted in The Taste of Angkor. It asks the home cook to buy the noodles rather than imitate the specialist fermentation and extrusion process without the proper equipment.
caveat: Prahok is the characteristic Cambodian fermented-fish seasoning; fish sauce alone makes a milder bowl but changes its depth. Use a commercially prepared prahok and boil it in the gravy rather than tasting it raw. Snakehead and other freshwater fish are common in Cambodia, while tilapia, catfish or cod are practical substitutes. The raw vegetable platter is integral to the dish, but choose only vegetables you can source fresh and safely; water lily stem and sesbania flowers may be omitted rather than replaced with decorative plants not sold as food.
prepNotes: Use only the pale tender lower core and cut it paper-thin before pounding or blending; coarse rings leave woody fibers in the gravy.
Flake the cooked fish with your fingers, then spread it on a plate and check again before pounding. A smooth gravy makes even a small bone noticeable.
Shred it directly into cold water acidulated with lime, then drain and dry it immediately before serving.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb firm white fish fillets, such as tilapia, catfish or cod
4 lemongrass stalks, tough layers removed and tender lower cores sliced very thin
1 1/2 inches fresh turmeric, peeled and sliced, or 2 tsp ground turmeric
1 1/2 inches galangal, peeled and sliced thin
5 makrut lime leaves, center ribs removed and sliced thin
1 to 2 tbsp commercially prepared prahok, to taste
2 tbsp fish sauce, plus more to taste
1 lb fresh round rice noodles or 12 oz dried medium rice vermicelli
1 small banana blossom, shredded, or 3 cups finely shredded green cabbage
2 cups bean sprouts, rinsed and dried
8 oz yard-long beans or green beans, sliced very thin
1 cup mixed mint, Thai basil and culantro leaves
steps: Put the fish, water and 1 teaspoon salt in a wide pot. Bring just to a simmer over medium heat, then lower the heat and poach gently 8 to 12 minutes, until the thickest piece is opaque and registers 145°F.
Lift the fish onto a plate and reserve every drop of broth. When cool enough to handle, remove skin and bones, flake the flesh and inspect it a second time for small bones.

Pound the lemongrass, turmeric, galangal, makrut lime leaves, shallots and garlic in a large mortar until moist and fibrous with no hard chunks. Alternatively, pulse in a food processor with 2 to 3 tablespoons reserved broth, scraping often; do not dilute it into a thin smoothie.
Add the flaked fish to the kroeung and pound or pulse briefly until the fish forms fine threads through the aromatic paste. This step gives body to the gravy without flour or starch.

Heat the oil in a clean heavy pot over medium heat. Add the fish-kroeung paste and cook 5 to 7 minutes, stirring continuously, until the raw shallot smell fades and the turmeric color deepens without browning hard on the bottom.

Whisk the prahok into 1 cup warm reserved fish broth, then strain through a fine sieve into the pot to catch coarse bones. Add the remaining broth, coconut milk, palm sugar, fish sauce and remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt.

Bring the gravy to a boil, lower to a steady simmer and cook uncovered 15 to 20 minutes. Checkpoint: the broth should be aromatic, pale yellow-green and lightly textured with fish, fluid enough to soak the noodles rather than as thick as curry sauce. Add water if it becomes heavy.

Taste a cooled spoonful. Add prahok or fish sauce sparingly for salinity and fermented depth, palm sugar only to round sharp edges, and water if the gravy tastes concentrated. Keep hot at a low simmer.

Prepare the noodles according to their package or vendor directions. Rinse rice noodles briefly in cool water, drain extremely well and gather them into six loose coils or bowls so they remain easy to portion.

While the noodles drain, shred the banana blossom directly into lime water, if using, then rinse and dry it. Arrange the blossom or cabbage, bean sprouts, cucumber, beans, herbs, lime wedges and sliced chiles on a large platter.

Divide noodles among six bowls and ladle over enough hot fish gravy to wet them generously without submerging them completely. Let each diner add a large handful of raw vegetables and herbs, lime and chile, then mix before eating.
Refrigerate gravy and noodles separately within 2 hours. Reheat the gravy to a boil and use within 3 days; prepare fresh raw vegetables for leftovers rather than storing them in the broth.

difficultyReason: Requires making a fine fresh kroeung, poaching and meticulously deboning fish, balancing fermented seasoning and coordinating noodles with several raw accompaniments.
